channel.title: Up First from NPR
channel.description:
NPR's Up First is the news you need to start your day. The three biggest stories of the day, with reporting and analysis from NPR News — in 10 minutes. Available weekdays at 6:30 a.m. ET, with hosts Leila Fadel, Steve Inskeep, Michel Martin and A Martinez. Also available on Saturdays at 9 a.m. ET, with Ayesha Rascoe and Scott Simon. On Sundays, hear a longer exploration behind the headlines with Ayesha Rascoe on "The Sunday Story," available by 8 a.m. ET. Subscribe and listen, then support your local NPR station at donate.npr.org.

Support public media by joining NPR+ at plus.npr.org. You’ll get perks for over 25 NPR podcasts, including sponsor-free listening for Up First, NPR News Now, and more.

item.title: Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
item.description:
President Trump says he pushed Nvidia to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO, raising questions about why the White House is getting involved in who runs a private company.
Nvidia gained nearly a trillion dollars in value after Huang returned, showing how much of the A-I economy is tied to one company and one man.
Russia’s war in Ukraine is spreading far beyond the battlefield, even as the Trump administration says talks toward a peace deal are making progress.

Want more analysis of the most important news of the day, plus a little fun? Subscribe to the Up First newsletter.

item.title: AI Impact On Economy, Russia-Ukraine War Spills Into Poland, No Deal At COP31
item.description:
The AI boom is driving huge investment across the economy, but the buildout is also pushing up prices and adding new pressure to inflation.
NATO holds an emergency meeting after three Russian cruise missiles entered Poland, as Warsaw pushes the alliance for more air defenses.
Global climate talks ended without an agreement on moving away from fossil fuels, leaving countries further from the targets they set a decade ago.

item.title: The booming cash advance industry trapping America’s small businesses
item.description:
What would you do if a financial deal you believed was a lifeline blew up your life? When a California entrepreneur landed in the world of merchant cash advances, he found America’s fastest-growing — and least regulated — source of funding for small businesses. Its daily payments and broken promises left him a changed man, back in his teenage bedroom, over $5 million in debt. NPR business correspondent Alina Selyukh joins The Sunday Story to trace his stubborn battle against an industry where borrowers rarely fight back.

item.title: AI Stocks Tumble, Permitting Reform Bill Clears Senate, Confusion Over Medicaid Cuts
item.description:
Financial markets suffer major losses as concerns over an AI bubble grow. A bipartisan bill that would speed up energy construction projects and weaken environmental regulations clears the US Senate. Confusion grows over new Medicaid work requirement rules set to begin in January.

item.title: Government Funding Pressure On Iran War, National Security & Tech, Iowa Detonation
item.description:
Democrats are weighing whether to use the government funding deadline to cut off money for the war in Iran, exposing divisions over how quickly the party should act.
The Trump administration approved sales of advanced U.S. chips to Chinese companies, including some the Pentagon has linked to China’s military, fueling a debate over whether those sales help America compete or create new security risks.
The Army delayed plans to destroy thousands of pounds of unstable bomb-making material in Iowa after public pressure and a lawsuit, even as officials warn colder weather could make it more dangerous.

Want more analysis of the most important news of the day, plus a little fun? Subscribe to the Up First newsletter.

item.title: Ben Shapiro reassesses the president he campaigned for | Newsmakers
item.description:
Conservative host Ben Shapiro says he is holding to his conservative values in the unstable era of President Trump.

The host of The Ben Shapiro Show voted against Trump in 2016 but also campaigned for him in 2024. He’s disappointed in the president’s tariffs, alleged corruption and the execution of the Iran war.

“I regret the way the president has performed,” Shapiro tells host Steve Inskeep in this episode of Newsmakers. “I don't regret my vote. I don't have a time machine.”

Shapiro says Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement and the general “whiff of corruption” that surrounds the White House — specifically the Trump family’s crypto company World Liberty Financial — all contributed to the Republican Party’s midterm losses in Congress, governor's mansions and state legislatures.

He believes that Republicans have an “uphill road in 2028” and that Vice President Vance isn’t the ideal Republican presidential candidate. He argues that Vance would shrink Trump’s winning 2024 voting bloc of Hispanics, the working class, women and college-educated individuals.

Shapiro points to Secretary of State Marco Rubio as a potential 2028 Republican candidate with broader appeal and a larger coalition. But he says many within the current White House will likely be damaged by association.

Shapiro also unpacks his new movie, Confession — featuring Rob Lowe and James Franco — and the recent decline in his show’s YouTube subscriptions.
